instagram_caption:
🚀 The $100B+ battle that blew up overnight: mRNA vs the rest.

In 2021 the vaccine market rewrote itself. Pfizer’s Comirnaty jumped from effectively $0 in 2020 to $36.8B in annual sales in 2021. Moderna — a biotech that was privately building a platform for years — vaulted to $18.5B the same year after its Spikevax roll-out. BioNTech, the small German partner, recognized roughly $14.8B in 2021 revenues tied to its Pfizer partnership. Meanwhile AstraZeneca, which pledged to sell broadly at cost early on, brought in about $3.0B and Johnson & Johnson reached roughly $1.1B.

Watch the timeline and you’ll see a classic chart-race story: fifteen years of zeros, then a surgical strip of explosive bars in 2021, then a sharp decline. 2022 still showed massive numbers (Pfizer ~$32.0B; Moderna ~$19.2B) as boosters and global delivery continued. By 2023 and 2024 those sums tapered hard — Pfizer to ~$22B then ~$12B, Moderna from $19.2B to $6.1B and down toward $3.2B in 2024. BioNTech slid too (from $14.8B to $2.5B across 2021–2024). AstraZeneca and J&J fell to near-zero as emergency demand and one-dose campaigns faded.

The drama isn’t just about money. It’s about platform bets: mRNA companies went from niche to household names in months, capturing the lion’s share of global COVID vaccine revenue and then being forced to navigate a post-emergency market where boosters, market saturation and new competitors cut prices and volume.

Headline: The mRNA Surge — how COVID vaccine sales blew up in 2021 and then receded.

In 2021 the market rebalanced almost overnight. Pfizer’s Comirnaty reached approximately $36.8 billion in sales, Moderna’s Spikevax ~$18.5 billion and BioNTech (partnered with Pfizer) about $14.8 billion. AstraZeneca, which supplied doses largely at-cost to many markets, reported roughly $3.0 billion in 2021 vaccine sales; Johnson & Johnson recorded about $1.1 billion. By 2022–2024 those annual revenues declined substantially as emergency demand eased: Pfizer’s vaccine revenue fell from $36.8B (2021) to an estimated $12.0B (2024); Moderna fell from $19.2B (2022) to ~$3.2B (2024).

This chart-race visualization maps the dramatic spike and subsequent wind-down across five major manufacturers. The data are compiled from company reports, regulatory disclosures and global delivery tallies. It’s a story of platform acceleration, geopolitical supply choices, and a market forced to move from emergency procurement to commercial reality.
